query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Earlier studies explored redesigning the bulk alloy, which risks compromising its original advantages, and several surface-modification approaches. Traditional thermal spraying and thermal plating produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding; composite coatings suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces; and laser cladding could generate intermetallic compounds, high residual stresses, cracks, and crazing. Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies reported improved hardness and wear resistance, but the broader requirements of compositional homogeneity, strong bonding, mechanical stability, and preservation of TC4’s beneficial properties remain. Formulate one neutral, testable hypothesis for an intervention that could satisfy these requirements. Specify the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a sequential surface treatment—first depositing a Ni60/WC composite coating by laser cladding on TC4 followed by plasma-based ion implantation (PBII) nitriding—will create a graded nitride layer that not only boosts the surface hardness and wear resistance by forming dense δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N phases on the top but also establishes a smooth diffusion transition (an α-Ti(N) sublayer) that preserves or even enhances fatigue performance relative to untreated TC4.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) alloy, which inherently has low hardness and poor wear resistance under extreme and high-contact-stress conditions.
generation.intervention: A two-step process: (1) Laser cladding a Ni60/WC composite coating onto the TC4 surface to introduce a high-hardness, wear-resistant layer, and (2) subjecting the cladded surface to PBII nitriding under controlled temperature and time conditions to induce the formation of nitrided phases and a hardness gradient.
generation.conditions: Process the TC4 samples under controlled laser cladding parameters to achieve a defect-free, ~50 µm thick composite coating and perform PBII nitriding (e.g., at 700–800 °C for durations optimized to produce a dual-domain nitride structure) under extreme-service conditions, including high-contact stress and cyclic loading environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructural gradient in which the outermost layer comprises hard nitride phases (δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N) formed by nitrogen diffusion, which gradually transitions into an α-Ti(N) solid solution that bridges the composite coating and the TC4 substrate.
generation.mechanism: The laser-clad Ni60/WC coating imparts high wear resistance due to in situ formed hard phases and good metallurgical bonding, while the subsequent PBII nitriding diffuses nitrogen into the coating and substrate, forming a graded nitride structure that introduces compressive residual stress and alleviates the brittleness (the 'eggshell effect') that can impair fatigue resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated TC4 and standalone laser cladding, the sequential treatment is predicted to raise the surface hardness by an estimated factor of three or more, reduce the friction coefficient and wear volume significantly, and maintain or improve the fatigue life through a smooth hardness gradient and enhanced interfacial toughness.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics of untreated TC4 alloy and those of TC4 with only the Ni60/WC laser-clad coating (which shows high hardness but may suffer from reduced fatigue toughness).
generation.boundary: The expected benefits are applicable under high-contact-stress and cyclic loading conditions; however, if PBII nitriding parameters (temperature, time, or ion fluence) are not optimized, adverse effects such as coating embrittlement or degradation of interfacial bonding might occur, limiting the performance gains.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from studies on Ni60/WC composite coatings (PMC10779869) and PBII nitriding on TC4 (PMC9785563) by integrating the two processes. The novel aspect is the sequential combination designed to engineer a graded nitride layer that mitigates the typical trade-off between high hardness and low fatigue resistance. The optimal nitriding parameters to ensure coating integrity remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of TC4 specimens and deposit a consistent Ni60/WC composite coating via laser cladding. Divide the samples into two groups: one group receives optimized PBII nitriding treatment (e.g., at 750 °C for a set duration) and the other group remains as laser-cladded only. Subject both groups to tribological tests (measuring friction coefficient and wear volume under high-contact loads) and fatigue tests (cyclic loading until failure) using standardized protocols.
measurements: Surface microhardness profile (nanoindentation across the coating depth)
Phase analysis (XRD to confirm formation of δ-TiN, ϵ-Ti2N, and α-Ti(N))
Residual stress mapping (XRD or Raman spectroscopy)
Tribological performance (friction coefficient and wear volume via pin-on-disc tests)
Fatigue life (number of cycles to failure under controlled cyclic loading)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sequential treatment (laser cladding followed by PBII nitriding) does not yield at least a 50% reduction in wear volume and a statistically significant improvement in fatigue life (comparable to or exceeding that of the laser-cladded-only baseline) relative to untreated TC4, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A metallurgical zirconium nitride (ZrN) layer was fabricated using glow metallurgy using nitriding with zirconiuming prior treatment of the Ti6Al4V alloy. The microstructure, composition and microhardness of the corresponding layer were studied. The influence of this treatment on fretting wear (FW) and fretting fatigue (FF) behavior of the Ti6Al4V alloy was studied. The composite layer consisted of an 8-μm-thick ZrN compound layer and a 50-μm-thick nitrogen-rich Zr–Ti solid solution layer. The surface microhardness of the composite layer is 1775 HK0.1. A gradient in cross-sectional microhardness distribution exists in the layer. The plasma ZrN metallurgical layer improves the FW resistance of the Ti6Al4V alloy, but reduces the base FF resistance. This occurs because the improvement in surface hardness results in lowering of the toughness and increasing in the notch sensitivity. Compared with shot peening treatment, plasma ZrN metallurgy and shot peening composite treatment improves the FW resistance and enhances the FF resistance of the Ti6Al4V alloy. The present results depict the preponderant role of temperature on both the structure and the mechanical behavior of the surface layers obtained during PBII surface treatments of Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy. Whatever the studied temperature, the PBII nitriding process resulted in the formation of two nitride domains. The most superficial one is a “composite” organization of δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N, while at depth an α-Ti(N) solid solution is formed. At the lowest studied temperatures (500 °C–700 °C), the response of these two domains to a nanoindentation test presents a continuous evolution of the property gradient with a strong hardening of the surface. The in-depth α-Ti(N) domain presents an increase of hardness with nitrogen insertion into the α-Ti structure, while much stronger changes are observed at the extreme surface, where a δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N composite is formed. The α-Ti(N) is expected to prevent the hard and fragile nitride surface layer from breaking (the eggshell effect). At 800 °C, the diffusion process becomes more efficient and leads to a plateau of medium hardness and a smooth mechanical properties gradient in the diffusion layer.
